beats.narration_text: Hi, this is Rohan Vijaykumar, from Humanitarians AI. A spectrogram is the picture audio people stare at when a waveform is not enough. Today I will teach you what that picture is measuring, when to use it, and the three things it will not tell you, even when it looks decisive.

props.command: What is a spectrogram actually measuring  -  when should I use one on a song, and what will it hide even when the picture looks decisive?
output: time across, frequency up, brightness as energy
use it to see structure you cannot hear as a shape
it drops phase, overlap, and anything under the floor

beats.narration_text: If you work with songs, speech, or lyrics tools, you will meet this picture. It is a map of energy over time and pitch. Use it to see structure. Do not use it as proof of what the sound is, or that a model understood the lyric.

show.event: Title lands: A map of energy.
Two faint axes fade in.
Subtitle: Use to see structure  -  not to prove what the sound is.

beats.narration_text: I am going to ask Claude to draw the map the honest way. No rainbow heat palette. Just the two axes, and energy as brightness. Watch the ask, then the result.

props.command: Draw a teaching spectrogram: horizontal time, vertical frequency, cell brightness as energy. Mark one sung vowel as a bright band. No rainbow colormap. Label the axes.

beats.narration_text: Time runs left to right. Frequency runs up. Each cell is how much energy sat in that pitch at that moment. A sung ah lights a band. Noise is speckle with no pitch to hold. You are looking at a histogram of loudness, sliced by time and by frequency.

show.event: Time axis draws left to right.
Frequency axis draws upward.
Grid of energy cells fills; one terracotta band for the sung ah.
Low-ink speckle labeled noise.

beats.narration_text: A sung ah is not one line. It is a stack: a lowest band, then fainter copies above it. Those copies are harmonics. Brightness is energy, not correctness. A bright smear can be a choir, distortion, or two notes fighting. Read the shape. Do not baptize it.

show.event: Title: A sung ah is a stack.
Lowest terracotta band, then fainter harmonic rows.
Caption: brightness is energy, not correctness.

beats.narration_text: The picture is made with a sliding window. A short window is sharp in time: you see the attack of a drum. A long window is sharp in pitch: you see a sung note sit still. You cannot have both at once. If a cut looks blurry, check the window before you blame the singer.

show.event: Title: The window is a trade.
Left grid: short window, blob in time.
Right grid: long window, thin pitch line.
Footer: you cannot have both at once.

beats.narration_text: What it hides. Phase: two sounds can share this picture and still cancel in the air. Overlapping voices smear into one stain. Quiet consonants fall under the floor. Use a spectrogram to find a note, a breath, a cut. Do not use it to decide a mix is clean, or that a model understood the lyric.

show.event: Three cards stack: Phase, Overlap, Floor.
Phase card gets the terracotta rail.
Footer: find a note  -  do not certify the mix.

beats.narration_text: The split is practical. Use a spectrogram to find a note, a breath, a cut, a buzz, a dropout. Do not hand it the last word on a clean mix, isolated stems, or understood lyrics. The picture is energy. Meaning is still on you.

show.event: Header: The split.
Left column: Use it to find.
Right column: Do not hand it.

beats.narration_text: Remember the split. A spectrogram shows energy by time and frequency. Use it when you need to see structure. Do not hand it the last word on phase, on overlapping sources, or on anything quieter than the floor.

artifactLines: Shows energy by time and frequency.
Use it to see structure you cannot hear as a shape.
Fails on phase, overlap, and anything under the floor.
